clue.text: Answer to this clue should be clearly stated

parts.words: Answer to this clue should be clearly stated
parts.note: surface reading: a quizmaster asking for a reply spoken plainly
setter's reading: this is 1 across, so its answer is literally placed across the grid

explanation.surface: A quizmaster asks for an answer to be spoken clearly.
explanation.walkthrough: PUT ACROSS means communicated effectively, and this answer is also put across the grid as 1 across.
explanation.definitionFit: To put something across is to communicate it successfully, so an idea put across has been conveyed plainly to listeners.

clue.text: Dish of fruit

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an attractive person, informally
second meaning: a soft downy stone fruit

explanation.surface: A bowl of fruit set on the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dish' is not crockery here but slang for a good-looking person.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a stone fruit with velvety skin and slang for a very attractive person, just as dish is.

clue.text: Cream and jam will be A1

parts.note: the cream of something is its top, the best part
to be in a jam is to be in a hole, a fix

explanation.surface: A scone with cream and jam will be first-rate.
explanation.walkthrough: Cream and jam look like a cream tea, but each is a synonym; TOP-HOLE is dated British slang for excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: A1 means first-class or excellent, as does the old-fashioned upper-class British exclamation of approval.

clue.text: Money spinner?

parts.note: surface reading: a venture that earns lots of cash
setter's reading: a piece of money that spins, as when tossed or twirled on a table

explanation.walkthrough: A money-spinner is a profitable scheme, but read literally it is money that spins: a COIN flipped at the start of a match.
explanation.definitionFit: A metal piece of currency is spun in the air when tossing heads or tails, so it is money that spins.

clue.text: Scottish resort where anything goes?

parts.note: surface reading: a permissive, wild holiday town
setter's reading: a place with nought by way of prohibition, the letter for zero followed by a word for a prohibition

explanation.surface: A Scottish seaside town with a reputation for no rules at all.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as O BAN, the name reads as zero ban, and where nothing is banned anything goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Oban is a harbour town and holiday destination on the west coast of Scotland, gateway to the islands.

clue.text: One i/c vessel — tramp is she, perhaps?

indicators.note: 'perhaps' says the words are only one possible version, so their letters may be arranged otherwise

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Asking who commands a ship, and whether that ship is a tramp steamer, called she.
explanation.walkthrough: A tramp is a cargo ship with no fixed route, and ships are called she, so the surface stays at sea; i/c means in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: A shipmaster is the captain of a merchant ship, the person in charge of the vessel.

clue.text: The man's father is said to be an immature person

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Wordsworth wrote that this is father of the man
second meaning: a young person not yet grown up

explanation.surface: Gossip that a man's father behaves like someone immature.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's line 'The Child is father of the Man' supplies the first meaning: character formed in youth shapes the adult.
explanation.definitionFit: A child is a young human not yet grown, and Wordsworth's poem famously calls it the parent of the adult.

clue.text: Swindle fellow out of money?

parts.note: a con is a swindle
tin is old British slang for money
short for gentleman, a fellow

explanation.surface: A conman cheats someone of their cash.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: the question mark admits the whole clue only hints at a swindle whose success depends on chance. Tin is old British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Contingent means dependent on chance or circumstance, and a swindle's success rests on the victim's fortune and trust.

clue.text: Is this housework decreasing?

parts.note: surface reading: getting smaller, as if the chores were shrinking
setter's reading: de-creasing, taking the creases out of clothes

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'decreasing' as de-creasing: the chore that removes creases is pressing clothes with a hot iron.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressing laundry with a heated iron is a household chore whose whole purpose is removing wrinkles from fabric.

clue.text: One name among party cronies calls the shots

indicators.note: 'among' places the first pair of items in the midst of what follows

parts.note: a do is a party
cronies are close friends
the Roman numeral for one
standard abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: One person among a group of party friends is the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: The pair goes in after the first letter of the cronies word, not at its edge; a do is everyday British for a party.
explanation.definitionFit: To call the shots is to be in control, and one who dominates exercises that control over others.

clue.text: Candidate's question paper?

parts.note: surface reading: the exam paper set for someone sitting a test
setter's reading: the document of questions filled in by someone applying for a job

explanation.walkthrough: Candidate and question paper suggest an exam, but the candidate is a job seeker and the paper full of questions is what they fill in.
explanation.definitionFit: A job applicant completes this printed document, answering its questions about experience and qualifications.

clue.text: Extremely hot over ridicule

indicators.note: 'over' asks for what comes before it to be turned over, read from the other end

parts.note: too means excessively, extremely
H marks the hot tap

explanation.surface: A complaint that something is far too hot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely hot' reads as one phrase, but it splits into TOO and H, and the pair is turned over to make HOOT.
explanation.definitionFit: To hoot is to jeer or derisively shout at someone, a noisy way of mocking them.

clue.text: When batting, duck's broken by boundary drive

parts.note: an ambit is a boundary or scope

indicators.note: 'broken by' means split apart with something set into the gap

parts.note: a batsman in cricket is said to be in
a duck is a score of nought in cricket, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A cricket report: a batsman out for nought, and a hit to the boundary.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket terms throughout: a duck is a score of zero, a boundary a hit to the edge, a drive a stroke; but drive is the definition. O goes inside IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Drive in the sense of motivation or determination to succeed is what ambition is.

clue.text: Constable's restraining hold broken by lout

indicators.note: 'restraining' means holding something in, so one part is held inside another

parts.note: a copper is a police officer, a constable

indicators.note: something broken is no longer in its original order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A police officer's grip on a suspect is broken by a thug.
explanation.walkthrough: Copper is everyday British slang for a police officer. The jumbled HOLD sits after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A clodhopper is a clumsy, boorish person, close in sense to an oaf or lout.

clue.text: Knight and queen involved at different stages in endgame

indicators.note: says the inserted items go in at separate points of the surrounding word rather than together

parts.note: only the first half, end, is wordplay here, and the end is the last; the second half is the definition
N is the chess notation for knight

indicators.note: 'involved' suggests tangled or complicated, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Chess pieces brought into play at different moments of an endgame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endgame' must be split into end and game, the second half being the definition. Lansquenet is an old German card game.
explanation.definitionFit: Lansquenet is a gambling card game of German origin, named after the mercenary foot soldiers who played it.

clue.text: Regarding the veins, say, is putting too much weight on!

parts.note: over means about, regarding, as in a row over money

indicators.note: 'say' tells us to go by how the word is spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: lodes are veins of ore in rock

explanation.surface: Talk of veins and someone straining under too much weight.
explanation.walkthrough: The veins are mineral seams, not blood vessels.
explanation.definitionFit: Overloads means burdens with more than can be carried, which is putting excessive weight on something.

clue.text: Doctor — paragon he to have established such an institution

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, altering its arrangement

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A saintly doctor founded a charitable home.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor looks like the founder, a medical man; it is the instruction to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An orphanage is the residential home for parentless children that a philanthropist might found, so it is such an institution.

clue.text: For pop concert, book this joint

parts.note: a gig is a live pop performance
OT, the Old Testament, is a book of the Bible

explanation.surface: Booking a venue for a pop concert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'book' looks like a verb meaning reserve, but it gives OT. A gigot is a leg of lamb or mutton.
explanation.definitionFit: Gigot is a leg of lamb or mutton, a cut of meat sold as a joint for roasting.

clue.text: Asked about work, little boy flinched

indicators.note: 'about' means turned around, so the word that follows reads from the other end

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
S is the abbreviation for small
Ed is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A little boy flinched when asked about his work.
explanation.walkthrough: Asked is the definition, as in posed a question. 'flinched' plays no part in the wordplay and seems only to complete the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To pose a question is to put or ask it, so posed can stand for asked.

clue.text: Dismissed, having carried on strike called

indicators.note: something carried is held within, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: to shed is to get rid of, dismiss
workers on strike are out

explanation.surface: Workers sacked after going on strike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dismissed' and 'on strike' both suggest a labour dispute; the first gives the outside, the second the inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Shouted means called out loudly, as when someone calls a name across a room.

clue.text: Animals' skins to be treated

indicators.note: something treated is processed and changed, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Animal hides waiting to be tanned.
explanation.walkthrough: Treating skins suggests tanning; here 'treated' rearranges the letters. Steinboks are small African antelopes.
explanation.definitionFit: Steinboks are small antelopes of southern and eastern Africa, so they are animals.

clue.text: Being too old, mean to have leader replaced

indicators.note: says the first letter is swapped out for a different one

parts.note: the mean is the average

explanation.surface: Someone past it, and spiteful to have their boss replaced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mean' looks like spiteful but is the statistical mean. Its first letter becomes O; the clue does not say which letter, so the definition must decide.
explanation.definitionFit: Overage describes someone older than the permitted limit, which is being too old.

clue.text: Has the shivers about game? That's a beastly tale

indicators.note: 'about' means surrounding, so one item goes round the other

parts.note: an ague is a fever with shivering fits
polo is a game played on horseback

explanation.surface: Someone shivering over a game, asked if it is a horrid story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beastly' looks like horrid but means with beasts in it: an apologue is a moral fable, typically about animals.
explanation.definitionFit: An apologue is a moral fable, often with animals as characters, like those of Aesop.

clue.text: Self-contained number, given backing, immediately succeeding

indicators.note: backing means moving in reverse, so the result is read from the end
'contained' means held inside, so the number holds something within it

parts.note: a number
the number's own self, written as a Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A self-contained flat number, backed by someone, following straight after.
explanation.walkthrough: The number contains itself: TEN holds X, ten in Roman numerals. 'Self-contained' looks like a property description.
explanation.definitionFit: Next means coming straight after, immediately following in order or time.

clue.text: The newspaper's job

parts.note: taken as written
the FT is the Financial Times

explanation.surface: A post at a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'job' looks like employment, but in criminal slang a job is a robbery.
explanation.definitionFit: In underworld slang a job is a crime such as a robbery, so a theft is a job.

clue.text: Fruit that's fleshy for the most part

indicators.note: 'for the most part' means nearly all, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: plump means well-padded, fleshy

explanation.surface: A fruit that is mostly flesh.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface describes juicy fruit, and the answer is one.
explanation.definitionFit: A plum is a sweet stone fruit with smooth purple or yellow skin.

clue.text: A slip of a girl

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a failure to hit, an error
second meaning: a young unmarried woman

explanation.walkthrough: 'A slip of a girl' is a set phrase for a slim young woman; split, it holds two meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A miss is a failed attempt or mistake, and also a title or term for a young unmarried woman.

clue.text: Mixed team line up at net for quarter final, perhaps

indicators.note: mixed means jumbled together, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A mixed doubles team lines up at the net for a tennis quarter final.
explanation.walkthrough: In a knockout the quarter final comes before the semi final and final, so it is third from last.
explanation.definitionFit: Antepenultimate means third from last, the position a quarter final holds in a knockout tournament.

clue.text: Water bird for ever consuming fish? Endlessly!

indicators.note: consuming means swallowing, so one item ends up inside another

parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: the ide is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A water bird endlessly eating fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird really does eat fish, which hides that 'fish' is wordplay; e'er is the poetic spelling poets use for ever.
explanation.definitionFit: The eider is a large sea duck, the source of eiderdown, so a bird of the water.

clue.text: Record of hours worked for two newspapers, mostly the first

indicators.note: only most of the first item is used, so it loses its last letter

parts.note: The Times, and sheet, a slang word for any newspaper

explanation.surface: Logging work hours on behalf of two newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Times loses its S, then SHEET follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A timesheet is a form on which an employee logs the hours they have spent working.
